Daniel’s three-way scheme is an interesting rediscovery, but it quietly conflates three different control knobs that phonetics keeps separate: **voicing** (are the vocal folds vibrating), **aspiration / voice onset time** (when voicing begins relative to a stop release), and **nasality** (whether the velum is lowered so air can escape through the nose). In many languages, “1 vs 2” is largely about VOT rather than a binary “no voicing vs voicing”: English /p t k/ are typically aspirated word-initially, while /b d g/ have shorter VOT and may be only partially voiced. And in **Mandarin specifically**, the Pinyin pairs *p/b, t/d, k/g, q/j, c/z* are standardly analyzed as **aspirated vs unaspirated voiceless** rather than voiceless vs voiced—so mapping them onto “voicing begins at release” risks misdescribing what Mandarin speakers are actually doing with their larynx (the tradition behind this is laid out cleanly in any IPA-based intro such as [Ladefoged & Johnson, *A Course in Phonetics*](https://www.cengage.com/c/a-course-in-phonetics-8e-ladefoged/)). His “physics not neural reflex” intuition isn’t crazy—laryngeal aerodynamics do create thresholds—but the timing is still actively controlled by muscles, and the aerodynamic story differs across places of articulation and loudness.

The “3” column is also framed as if nasals are defined by “voicing starts before the plosive,” but nasals are better thought of as **a separate manner**: they are “stop-like” closures in the mouth **plus an open velopharyngeal port**, which is why the airflow route changes. That makes the later “_LF: nasal sound impossible” claim too strong. It’s true that most fricatives resist nasalization because nasal airflow reduces the oral pressure needed for strong frication, but “impossible” is more categorical than the evidence warrants: languages do have contrastive nasalization on vowels and approximants, and various “nasalized fricative” phenomena exist at least allophonically. Likewise, “mouth volume decreases: m > …” feels like a proxy for something real (acoustic resonance and oral cavity shape), but **nasality is controlled primarily by the velum**, not by mouth volume; cavity size mostly changes *timbre*, not whether nasal airflow is available.

Finally, the “H is confusing” point is a gift: it exposes how orthography smuggles in assumptions. English *h* is typically a **glottal fricative** ([h])—often closer to “voicelessness on a vowel” than a full-blown consonant—whereas Mandarin Pinyin *h* is usually **velar/uvular frication** ([x]~[χ]) depending on speaker and context. So if Daniel is using one “H” bucket across “Western” and Pinyin, the puzzle may be less about mechanism and more about mixing two different sounds under one letter—exactly the kind of trap the [IPA chart](https://www.internationalphoneticassociation.org/IPAcharts/inter_chart_2018/IPA_2018.html) was designed to avoid.
